definition.text: A set of water management practices, also called SuDS, that make modern drainage work with natural water processes as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy.

facts.text: SuDS aim to reduce the harm development does to the natural water cycle, especially surface runoff and water pollution.
When vegetation is replaced by concrete, asphalt and roofs, land loses its ability to absorb rain, which then overloads drains and causes floods.
SuDS often bypass traditional drains and return rainwater to natural water bodies as soon as possible.
Typical components include bioswales, permeable paving, artificial wetlands, retention basins, green roofs, rain gardens and downspout disconnection.
Plants and soil remove stormwater pollutants by adsorption, filtration and plant uptake.
In urban areas covered mostly by hard surfaces, more than half of the rain becomes runoff.
Planting a rain garden to handle drainage usually costs less than digging tunnels and laying pipes.
Drainage systems have been found in ancient cities more than 5,000 years old, but modern systems appeared only in 19th-century Western Europe, mainly to deal with sewage.

definition.text: An artificial pond, also called a wet pond, with plants around its edge and a permanent pool of water, used to manage stormwater.

facts.text: It is used to control runoff, protect against floods and erosion, and improve the quality of nearby water.
It differs from a detention basin or 'dry pond', which holds water only after a storm and then drains at a controlled rate.
It also differs from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

definition.text: The removal of pollutants and sediment from stormwater runoff by a planted soil area.

facts.text: A bioretention cell aims to reduce peak runoff and remove pollutants.
A typical cell has a sand bed, layers of filter media and plants on top; stored water seeps into the soil below over several days.
The name refers to plants and bacteria in the media that hold, absorb, break down and cycle contaminants.
Filtration, adsorption, chemical change and biological breakdown are its main ways of treating pollutants.
Untreated nitrogen and phosphorus in runoff cause eutrophication downstream; well-designed media can sharply reduce both.
In laboratory tests, cells removed 94% of zinc, 88% of copper, 95% of lead and more than 95% of cadmium at typical stormwater levels.
Its capacity for heavy metals is limited, so the media must eventually be replaced where metal loads are high.
Soils with more than 25 percent clay, slopes over 20 percent or unstable ground may rule it out.

definition.text: A channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution.

facts.text: It is a drainage course with gently sloped sides of less than 6%.
It is designed to keep water in the swale as long as safely possible, since longer stays remove more pollutants.
Plants catch pollutants, which then enter the soil and are broken down by bacteria.
Bioswales can also recharge groundwater, reduce flooding and erosion and give pollinators habitat.
They suit streets and parking lots, where car pollution is washed off by the first rain.
There are four types: low grass, vegetated, low water use and wet bioswales.
Poor maintenance can lead to high repair costs, so inspection at least once a year is advised.
In 1996, 2330 lineal feet of bioswale were installed at Willamette River Park in Portland, and check dams cut suspended solids entering the river by 50%.

definition.text: The first runoff of a rainstorm, which washes off pollution that has built up on hard surfaces.

facts.text: Urban and suburban first-flush runoff is described as highly toxic.
Bioswales are built to handle the first flush, so they suit roads, parking lots and roofs.
Rainwater tanks may use a first-flush diverter to keep contaminants out of stored water.
